Group theory OurBigBook.com
For a subgroup H of finite index, choose representatives t of right cosets Ht. Write tg=h(t,g)tg​ with h(t,g)∈H. The transfer is VG,H​(g)=∏t​h(t,g)(modH′). Replacing t by at​t multiplies each factor by at​ on the left and atg​−1​ on the right; these cancel in the abelianization because t↦tg​ is a permutation. Burnside transfer theorem (P⊆Z(NG​(P))⟹G has a normal p-complement)

Words: 157 Articles: 1
Transfer (group theory) OurBigBook.com
The hypothesis makes P abelian and makes any two conjugate elements of P equal. For the latter assertion, Sylow conjugacy inside the centralizer of the target element adjusts a conjugating element into NG​(P), where it centralizes P. Evaluating group transfer to P on an element u∈P, each coset cycle contributes a conjugate of u raised to the cycle length, hence that same power of u. The restriction is consequently u↦u[G:P], an automorphism of the abelian p-group. Transfer is surjective, and its kernel is the required normal p-complement.

Cyclic Sylow subgroup at the least prime gives a normal complement

Words: 65
Burnside transfer theorem OurBigBook.com
Let p be the smallest prime dividing the order of a finite group, and suppose its Sylow subgroup P is cyclic of order pa. Conjugation embeds NG​(P)/CG​(P) into Aut(P), of order pa−1(p−1). Since P⊆CG​(P), this quotient has order prime to p. Its remaining possible prime divisors are smaller than p and cannot divide ∣G∣. Thus NG​(P)=CG​(P), and the Burnside transfer theorem gives a normal p-complement.

Prüfer rank (rkP​(G)=supH≤G, H finitely generated​d(H))

Words: 141 Articles: 1
Group theory OurBigBook.com
The Prüfer rank bounds the number of generators of a group needed for each finitely generated subgroup, without requiring the ambient group to be finitely generated. The additive group Q has Prüfer rank one: any finitely generated subgroup has a common denominator and is cyclic, but no finite collection generates all rational numbers. Prüfer rank cannot increase under taking subgroups or quotients; for quotients, lift a finite generating set and apply the rank bound to the subgroup generated by its lifts.

Prüfer rank OurBigBook.com
For a normal subgroup N with Prüfer rank r and quotient of rank s, let H=⟨h1​,…,hk​⟩≤G. Choose at most s elements xj​∈H generating the image of H. Write hi​=wi​(x1​,…,xs​)ni​ with ni​∈N∩H. The finitely generated subgroup ⟨n1​,…,nk​⟩ needs at most r generators, so H needs at most r+s. The full intersection H∩N need not be finitely generated.

Maximal condition on subgroups (max)

Words: 85
Group theory OurBigBook.com
A group has the maximal condition on subgroups when every ascending sequence of subgroups eventually stabilizes. Equivalently, every subgroup is a finitely generated group. If a subgroup were not finitely generated, repeatedly adjoining an element outside the previously generated subgroup would give a strictly ascending sequence. Conversely, generators of the union of an ascending sequence all lie in one term, making that term the whole union. This condition is preserved by group extensions because each subgroup is an extension of its intersection with the kernel by its image in the quotient.

A group action is free when only the identity fixes any given point, or equivalently every stabilizer subgroup is trivial. The trivial group acts freely on every space. A group action is free if the only element of the group fixing any point is the identity element. Thus every stabilizer subgroup is trivial. This is a property of an action of any group, not an assertion that the acting group is a free group.

Finite groups cannot act freely on Euclidean space

Free group action OurBigBook.com
If a nontrivial finite group acted freely on Rn, a prime-order cyclic subgroup Cp​ would too. The quotient is an n-manifold with contractible universal cover. The singular version of cellular free resolution from a contractible universal cover identifies its cohomology with group cohomology of Cp​. The periodic resolution of a finite cyclic group gives H2j(Cp​;Z)=Z/p for every j≥1. But Poincaré duality for noncompact manifolds makes the quotient cohomology zero above dimension n. This contradiction excludes the action, for arbitrary homeomorphisms, not only Euclidean isometries.

Degree of homeomorphisms defines a homomorphism into {1,−1}, whose kernel is trivial, since no nonidentity action map can have degree one. Thus the acting group has order at most two. For S0, freeness on its two points gives the same conclusion directly.

This constructs a Eilenberg–MacLane space K(G,1) with only one (n+1)-cell. The one-cell bound on next-degree cohomology gives dimension at most one in degree n+1. The modern types are affine (HA), almost simple (AS), simple diagonal (SD), compound diagonal (CD), product action (PA), holomorph simple (HS), holomorph compound (HC), and twisted wreath (TW). Intransitive and imprimitive maxima are respectively unequal-part subset stabilizers and block-system stabilizers. For each such N, some iterate satisfies θ−m(N)=N, so kerθ⊆kerθm⊆N. Intersecting proves the inclusion. Consequently every finitely generated residually finite group is a Hopfian group.

If K is a finitely generated group, then the semidirect product K⋊H is a residually finite group exactly when both K and H are residually finite groups. To separate an element whose H coordinate is nontrivial, use a finite quotient of H. For 1=k∈K, choose a finite-index normal subgroup U omitting k, and intersect all subgroups of index at most [K:U] to obtain a characteristic finite-index subgroup C≤U. The induced map into (K/C)⋊im(H→Aut(K/C)) has finite target and separates k. More generally, finite generation can be replaced by a separating family of finite-index normal subgroups invariant under the given H action.

A group G is conjugacy separable when any two nonconjugate elements remain nonconjugate in some finite quotient. Equivalently, every conjugacy class is closed in the profinite topology.

Every subgroup of a residually finite group is residually finite, because a finite quotient separating an element of the ambient group also separates it after restriction to the subgroup.

For a prime number p, reducing every entry modulo p defines a group homomorphism from an integral matrix group to the corresponding matrix group over Fp​. The target is finite. An infinite residually finite group is not a simple group. For a nonidentity element, residual finiteness supplies a map to a finite group in which it survives. Its kernel is proper and cannot be trivial, since an infinite group cannot inject into a finite group.

A group is a torsion group when every element is a torsion element, meaning that each element has finite order. The orders need not have a common finite bound. A torsion group has no nontrivial torsion-free group as a subgroup; in particular it cannot contain a nonabelian free group. Infinite finitely generated groups of this kind can be constructed using a torsion group construction by p-power relators.

The Golod-Shafarevich infinitude criterion for pro-p groups makes the resulting pro-p group infinite. Its abstract subgroup generated by the two generator images is dense and infinite; each element is represented by an enumerated word and has finite order. The ambient finite quotients separate its elements, so it is also a residually finite group. The abstract subgroup, rather than the whole topological group, is the desired finitely generated torsion group.

A group is locally finite when every subgroup that is a finitely generated group is finite. It is a torsion group, since the cyclic subgroup generated by one element must be finite. The torsion subgroup of an abelian group consists of all elements of finite order. For a finitely generated abelian group, it is the finite direct summand complementary to the free abelian part.

In a finite abelian group, every nonempty fiber of this homomorphism has cardinality ∣G[m]∣, so ∣G:mG∣=∣G[m]∣. This follows directly: if mx=my, then x−y∈G[m], and conversely translating by an element of G[m] leaves the image unchanged. On the cyclic group ZN​, the solutions of mx=0 number gcd(m,N); divide both integers by their greatest common divisor to see that x must be a multiple of N/gcd(m,N).

If finite normal subgroups H,K of a group have coprime orders, their intersection is trivial by Lagrange's theorem. For h∈H and k∈K, the commutator hkh−1k−1 belongs to both subgroups: write it as h(kh−1k−1) to use normality of H, and as (hkh−1)k−1 to use normality of K. Hence it is the identity and hk=kh. For a finite group with Sylow p-subgroup P, a normal p-complement is a normal subgroup of order ∣G∣/∣P∣. It consists exactly of the elements of order prime to p: every such element has trivial image in the p-group quotient, and every element of the complement has prime-to-p order. A finite group is p-nilpotent when it has a normal p-complement. This terminology is distinct from having a normal Sylow p-subgroup. A finite group is nilpotent exactly when it is p-nilpotent for every prime dividing its order.

If a prime p divides the degree of every nonlinear irreducible character of a finite group, the group has a normal p-complement. Indeed, the p-prime-degree characters are exactly the linear characters. Their squared-degree sum is ∣G:G′∣, whose p-part is ∣G:G′∣p​; Isaacs' character-degree criterion for p-nilpotency applies.

Invariant p-prime-degree characters of N extend, and each has exactly h extensions of p-prime degree. Conjugation by the p-group G/N then gives s/h≡∣N∣(modp). A subnormal series is a finite chain of subgroups in which each is a normal subgroup of the next. A member need not be normal in the whole group. Requiring the factors to be cyclic groups defines a polycyclic group; allowing finite factors as well defines a poly-(cyclic or finite) group.

Any two finite subnormal series have refinements with the same successive factors up to ordering and group isomorphism. For descending chains Ai​ and Bj​, insert Ai+1​(Ai​∩Bj​) between Ai​ and Ai+1​ and insert Bj+1​(Bj​∩Ai​) in the other chain. The Zassenhaus butterfly lemma identifies the factor indexed by (i,j) in the first refinement with the factor indexed by (j,i) in the second. If both chains are composition series, their simple factors admit no nontrivial refinement, giving the Jordan–Hölder theorem.

A normal series is a chain 1=G0​≤G1​≤⋯≤Gr​=G whose terms are all normal subgroups of the ambient group. A subnormal series only requires each term normal in the next. Confusing these conditions would incorrectly require every term of a composition series to be normal in the full group.

A chief series is a strict normal series of a group with no proper normal-series refinement. Its factors are minimal normal subgroups of the appropriate quotient groups. A chief factor of a finite soluble group is elementary abelian, whereas a composition factor of a finite soluble group is cyclic of prime order. A chief factor can therefore have order larger than a prime.

A chief factor of G is a quotient N/M with M,N normal in G and no G-normal subgroup strictly between them. Equivalently, N/M is a minimal normal subgroup of G/M. Such factors are the successive factors of a chief series, and are direct products of isomorphic simple groups when G is finite.

Words: 299 Articles: 3
Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
A minimal normal subgroup is a nontrivial normal subgroup containing no smaller nontrivial normal subgroup of the ambient group. It need not be a minimal nontrivial subgroup. In a finite soluble group, it is elementary abelian: its derived subgroup must be trivial, a characteristic Sylow subgroup selects one prime, and the characteristic subgroup of elements killed by that prime gives exponent p.

Minimal normal subgroups of finite solvable groups are elementary abelian

Words: 45
Minimal normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
A nontrivial minimal normal subgroup N of a finite solvable group is abelian: its commutator subgroup is characteristic, and minimality plus solvability excludes N′=N. A nontrivial Sylow subgroup of this abelian group is characteristic, so minimality makes N a p-group. The characteristic subgroup of pth powers is proper, hence trivial by minimality. Therefore N is an elementary abelian group.

Words: 115
Minimal normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
Choose a minimal nontrivial normal subgroup L of K. Its conjugates under the ambient group are minimal normal subgroups of K; distinct ones intersect trivially and commute. Choose a maximal family whose product is direct. Any omitted conjugate either lies in that product or meets it trivially and could be adjoined, so all conjugates lie in it. Their product is ambient-normal and therefore is K. A normal subgroup of one factor is then normal in K, since the other factors commute with it; minimality makes each factor simple. All factors are isomorphic because they are conjugates of L. In the abelian case they are cyclic of one common prime order.

Words: 79
Minimal normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
The socle is generated by all minimal nontrivial normal subgroups. Distinct minimal normal subgroups commute and meet trivially, although in the abelian case not every collection of them is an independent direct-product decomposition. It is a direct product of simple groups. In a faithful primitive permutation group each nontrivial normal subgroup is transitive; its minimal normal subgroups are either elementary abelian and regular, or direct powers of a nonabelian simple group. This is the starting point of the O'Nan–Scott theorem.

Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
If N={1,z} is a normal subgroup of a group G, conjugation by any element of G preserves N and fixes 1. It must therefore fix z as well. Thus N lies in the center of a group. This fact can turn a small normal subgroup into a commuting factor without assuming the whole group is abelian.

For two distinct points of the Riemann sphere, conjugate by a Möbius transformation sending them to zero and infinity. A transformation fixing those two points has the form z↦λz, λ=0. Composition multiplies the parameter, so the pointwise stabilizer is isomorphic to the complex multiplicative group. For zero and one, conjugation by z/(1−z) gives z↦λz/[1+(λ−1)z].

The Möbius transformations preserving a three-point set act faithfully on it: one fixing all three is the identity. Every permutation is realized because a Möbius transformation can send any ordered distinct triple to any other, by composing the two normalizations to 0,1,∞. For that normalized set the six maps are z, 1−z, 1/z, 1/(1−z), z/(z−1) and (z−1)/z. Thus its setwise stabilizer is the symmetric group S3​. Normalizing any other three-point set conjugates its stabilizer to this group.

If every nonidentity element of a finite group has order equal to a prime p, its order is a power of p. For any prime divisor q of the group order, Cauchy theorem for groups gives an element of order q, forcing q=p. This statement does not imply that the group is abelian; odd-characteristic upper unitriangular groups provide counterexamples.

Finite subgroup of a field multiplicative group is cyclic

Words: 42
Exponent of a finite group OurBigBook.com
Every finite subgroup of K× is cyclic. If its exponent is m, all its elements are roots of Xm−1, so its size is at most m; finite abelian group theory supplies an element of order m, forcing equality.

Order of an element of a finite group

Words: 33
Group theory OurBigBook.com
The order of an element is the least positive power equal to the identity and divides the order of a finite group.
This is the order of a group element in the finite setting, one use of order (group theory).

Order (group theory)

Words: 43
Group theory OurBigBook.com
In group theory, order can mean the cardinality of a group or the least positive n for which a group element g satisfies gn=e. If no such n exists, the element has infinite order. For a finite group, Lagrange's theorem implies that each element order divides the group order.
